lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Isn't this Heracles? No one else, by Heracles. The bow, the club, the lion-skin, the size — it's all Heracles. So a son of Zeus has died? Tell me, glorious victor, are you dead? I used to sacrifice to you on earth as if you were a god.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: And rightly so. The real Heracles is up in heaven with the gods, married to Hebe of the lovely ankles, and I'm just his shade.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What are you saying? The god's shade? Can someone be half a god and dead in the other half?

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Yes. He didn't die. I, his image, did.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I see. He handed you over to Pluto as his stand-in, so you're the one who's dead in his place.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Something like that.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: How did the meticulous Aeacus not spot you weren't the real thing and accept this substitute Heracles?

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Because I looked exactly like him.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: True. Exactly enough to be him. But watch out — maybe it's the other way around and you're the real Heracles, while the shade is up there married to Hebe with the gods.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You're bold and a chatterbox. If you don't stop mocking me, you'll soon learn what kind of god's shade I am.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Your bow's out and ready. But what do I have to fear from you? I'm already dead. [pause] Still, tell me by your Heracles: when he was alive, were you with him even then, as a shade? Or were you one in life, and when you died you split — the one flew off to the gods, and you, the shade, came to Hades as was fitting?

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: I shouldn't even answer a man who pesters me like this. But listen anyway: As much as Amphitryon was in Heracles, that part died, and I am all of it. What was Zeus's stays with the gods in heaven.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Clear as day now. So Alcmene gave birth to two Heracleses at once — one to Amphitryon, one to Zeus — and you two were secret twin brothers.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: No, you fool. We were the same person.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Hard to grasp, two composite Heracleses, unless you were fused like a centaur, man and god in one.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Don't we all seem made of two parts to you — soul and body? So what's stopping the soul, which was from Zeus, from being in heaven, while mortal me is here with the dead?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But, my dear son of Amphitryon, that would work if you had a body. Now you're a bodiless shade. So you're in danger of making Heracles triple already.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Triple? How?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: This way: one in heaven, you here as the shade, and the body dissolved into dust. That's three. And think what father you'll invent for the third.

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You're bold and a sophist. Who are you, anyway?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: The shade of Diogenes of Sinope. But not me, by Zeus — not among the immortal gods. I'm here with the best of the dead, laughing at Homer and all that frigid nonsense.
